# What a Determinant Measures

One scalar answers three questions about a square matrix transformation

- [A determinant is a signed scale factor](#a-determinant-is-a-signed-scale-factor)
- [Familiar transformations tell the story](#familiar-transformations-tell-the-story)
- [In two dimensions, $ad-bc$ is signed area](#in-two-dimensions-ad-bc-is-signed-area)
- [Why the area is $\abs{ad-bc}$](#area-proof)

## A determinant is a signed scale factor

Let $\mat{A}\in\reals^{n\times n}$ and
$T_{\mat{A}}(\vct{x})=\mat{A}\vct{x}$

Let $\mathcal S\subseteq\reals^n$ be a measurable region: a set of
column-vector points, not a matrix

Its image under the transformation is

$$
T_{\mat{A}}(\mathcal S)
=\{\mat{A}\vct{x}:\vct{x}\in\mathcal S\}
$$

Then

$$
\operatorname{vol}_n\bigl(T_{\mat{A}}(\mathcal S)\bigr)
=\abs{\det(\mat{A})}\operatorname{vol}_n(\mathcal S)
$$

- $\abs{\det(\mat{A})}$ is the $n$-dimensional volume scale factor
- $\det(\mat{A})>0$ preserves orientation
- $\det(\mat{A})<0$ reverses orientation
- $\det(\mat{A})=0$ collapses at least one dimension

::: {.key-point}
The determinant records [scale, orientation, and collapse]{.alert} in one number
:::

::: {.notes}
Each $\vct{x}\in\mathcal S$ is a column vector, and $\mat{A}$ acts on every
such point. If a polygon or polytope is described by a finite vertex matrix,
place its vertex vectors in the columns so that left multiplication by
$\mat{A}$ transforms all vertices at once.
:::

## Familiar transformations tell the story

| Transformation in $\reals^2$ | Determinant | Geometric effect |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| $\operatorname{diag}(s,t)$ | $st$ | area scales by $\abs{st}$ |
| $\begin{bmatrix}1&c\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ | $1$ | a shear changes shape, not area |
| rotation $\mat{R}_\theta$ | $1$ | area and orientation are preserved |
| reflection $\mat{H}$ | $-1$ | area is preserved; orientation reverses |
| projection onto a line $\mat{Q}$ | $0$ | the plane collapses to a line |

The sign distinguishes transformations that have the same area scale but opposite orientation

## In two dimensions, $ad-bc$ is signed area

The columns are the images of the standard basis vectors:

$$
\mat{A}
=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}\vct{A}_1&\vct{A}_2\end{bmatrix}
$$

The image of the unit square is the parallelogram with edge vectors
$\vct{A}_1$ and $\vct{A}_2$, and

$$
\det(\mat{A})=ad-bc,
\qquad
\text{parallelogram area}=\abs{ad-bc}
$$

- swapping the two columns reverses orientation and changes the sign
- dependent columns collapse the parallelogram and give determinant zero

## Why the area is $\abs{ad-bc}$ {#area-proof}

Use $\vct{A}_1=(a,c)^{\mathsf T}$ as the base and
$\vct{A}_2=(b,d)^{\mathsf T}$ as the other edge

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
Base length and a perpendicular unit vector

\begin{gather*}
L=\sqrt{a^2+c^2}>0,
\qquad \vct{n}=\frac1L\begin{bmatrix}-c\\a\end{bmatrix}\\
\vct{A}_1^{\mathsf T}\vct{n}=0,
\qquad \vct{n}^{\mathsf T}\vct{n}=1
\end{gather*}
:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
Height = magnitude of the perpendicular component

\begin{align*}
h&=\abs{\vct{A}_2^{\mathsf T}\vct{n}}\\
&=\frac{\abs{-bc+ad}}{L}
\end{align*}
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
$$
\text{Area}=\text{base}\times\text{height}
=L\frac{\abs{ad-bc}}{L}=\abs{\det(\mat{A})}
$$
:::

- $L=0$: the first edge is zero, so both area and determinant are zero
- $\vct{n}$ points left of the directed base: $ad-bc>0$ for the other edge
  on the left, $ad-bc<0$ on the right

::: {.notes}
The dot product with a unit vector gives the signed component in that
direction: $\vct{A}_2^{\mathsf T}\vct{n}
=\lVert\vct{A}_2\rVert\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between
the second edge and the normal. Its absolute value is the perpendicular
distance between the parallel sides. This uses elementary projection
geometry, independently of any determinant-area formula. If the edges are
collinear, the height and determinant are both zero.

For larger matrices, elimination is our computational route.
:::

# Compute by Elimination

The determinant follows the same row operations already used for systems,
inverses, and PLU

- [Three row operations control the determinant](#three-row-operations-control-the-determinant)
- [Triangular matrices end the computation](#triangular-matrices-end-the-computation)
- [The PLU example already contains the determinant](#the-plu-example-already-contains-the-determinant)
- [Read the determinant from PLU](#read-the-determinant-from-plu)
- [Read the sign directly from a permutation](#read-the-sign-directly-from-a-permutation)
- [Try it by elimination](#try-it-by-elimination)

::: {.notes}
This compact treatment intentionally omits general cofactor expansion,
adjugates, and Cramer's rule. If recognition of those topics is later needed
for Anton alignment, add it as optional material rather than making it the
default computational route.
:::

## Three row operations control the determinant

| Row operation | Effect on the determinant |
|:---|:---|
| $R_i\leftrightarrow R_j$ | multiply by $-1$ |
| $R_i\leftarrow cR_i$, $c\ne0$ | multiply by $c$ |
| $R_i\leftarrow R_i+cR_j$, $i\ne j$ | no change |

The analogous rules hold for column operations

::: {.key-point}
Use row replacement freely; track every row swap and scaling
:::

## Triangular matrices end the computation

For an upper-triangular matrix,

$$
\mat{U}=
\begin{bmatrix}
u_{11}&u_{12}&\cdots&u_{1n}\\
0&u_{22}&\cdots&u_{2n}\\
\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&\cdots&0&u_{nn}
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\det(\mat{U})=\prod_{j=1}^n u_{jj}
$$

The same diagonal-product rule holds for lower-triangular matrices

To compute $\det(\mat{A})$:

1. Eliminate to triangular form using row replacements and swaps
2. Avoid normalizing pivot rows; otherwise track the scaling
3. If elimination used $s$ swaps, then
   $\det(\mat{A})=(-1)^s\prod_{j=1}^n u_{jj}$

## The PLU example already contains the determinant

Return to the example from
[Matrix Transformations]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#elimination-becomes-a-factorization):

$$
\mat{A}=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&0&1\\
2&2&0\\
1&3&1
\end{bmatrix}
\quad\xrightarrow[\text{row replacement}]{\text{two row swaps}}\quad
\mat{U}=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&2&0\\
0&2&1\\
0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore

$$
\det(\mat{A})=(-1)^2(2)(2)(1)=4
$$

## Read the determinant from PLU

For square matrices of the same size, $\det(\mat{B}\mat{C})=\det(\mat{B})\det(\mat{C})$

Apply this product rule to $\mat{A}=\mat{P}\mat{L}\mat{U}$:

$$
\det(\mat{A})
=\det(\mat{P})\det(\mat{L})\det(\mat{U})
=(-1)^s\prod_{j=1}^n u_{jj}
$$

- $s$: number of row swaps in the factorization
- $\det(\mat{P})=(-1)^s$: each row swap reverses the sign
- $\det(\mat{L})=1$: unit lower triangular

## Read the sign directly from a permutation

Read column $j$: its $1$ in row $i$ means $\mat{P}\vct{e}_j=\vct{e}_i$

$$
\mat{P}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}
\qquad 1\longmapsto2\longmapsto3\longmapsto1
$$

- A cycle of length $k$ takes $k-1$ swaps: sign $(-1)^{k-1}$
- Here: one cycle of length $3$, so $\det(\mat{P})=(-1)^2=1$
- Count fixed indices as cycles of length $1$

::: {.key-point}
For $c$ disjoint cycles on $n$ indices: $\det(\mat{P})=(-1)^{n-c}$

No need to carry out row swaps back to $\mat{I}$
:::

## Try it by elimination

$$
\mat{B}=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&1&0\\
4&3&1\\
2&2&3
\end{bmatrix},
$$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Compute $\det(\mat{B})$ using row replacements and swaps, but no pivot-row scaling.
<span class="exsub">Which operations change the determinant?</span>
<span class="exsub">Does your result show that $\mat{B}$ is invertible?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Use $R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1$, then
$R_3\leftarrow R_3-R_1$, then $R_3\leftarrow R_3-R_2$. The resulting upper-
triangular matrix has diagonal entries $2,1,2$. No operation changes the
determinant, so $\det(\mat{B})=4\ne0$ and $\mat{B}$ is invertible.
:::

# What the Determinant Reveals

The value connects computation, geometry, and matrix algebra

- [Nonzero determinant means invertible](#nonzero-determinant-means-invertible)
- [Products multiply signed scale factors](#products-multiply-signed-scale-factors)
- [Eigenvalues give another determinant formula](#eigenvalues-give-another-determinant-formula)
- [Compute only what the problem requires](#compute-only-what-the-problem-requires)

## Nonzero determinant means invertible

For a square matrix $\mat{A}\in\reals^{n\times n}$,

\begin{align*}
\det(\mat{A})\ne0
&\iff \mat{A}\text{ has }\,n\text{ pivots}\\
&\iff \mat{A}^{-1}\text{ exists}\\
&\iff \text{for every }\vct{b}\in\reals^n,
   \ \mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}\text{ has exactly one solution}
\end{align*}

Likewise,

$$
\det(\mat{A})=0
\iff \mat{A}\vct{z}=\vct{0}
\text{ for some }\vct{z}\ne\vct{0}
$$

That nonzero direction collapses to $\vct{0}$

::: {.key-point}
The determinant summarizes a conclusion that elimination already reveals
:::

## Products multiply signed scale factors

First $\mat{A}$ acts, then $\mat{B}$ acts:

$$
\vct{x}\longmapsto\mat{A}\vct{x}
\longmapsto\mat{B}\mat{A}\vct{x}
$$

Their signed scale factors multiply:

$$
\det(\mat{B}\mat{A})
=\det(\mat{B})\det(\mat{A})
$$

Consequently, for $k=1,2,\ldots$,

$$
\det(\mat{I})=1,
\qquad
\det(\mat{A}^k)=\det(\mat{A})^k
$$

If $\mat{A}$ is invertible, then
$\det(\mat{A}^{-1})=1/\det(\mat{A})$

## Eigenvalues give another determinant formula

An [eigenvector]{.alert} is a nonzero vector that $\mat{A}$ maps to a scalar
multiple of itself:

$$
\mat{A}\vct{v}=\lambda\vct{v},
\qquad \vct{v}\ne\vct{0}
$$

The scale factor $\lambda$ is the corresponding [eigenvalue]{.alert}

[Eigenvalues]({{< meta decks.d07.file >}}) will develop this idea

Counting repeated eigenvalues and allowing complex values,

$$
\det(\mat{A})=\lambda_1\lambda_2\cdots\lambda_n
$$

- a zero eigenvalue is equivalent to a zero determinant
- for triangular $\mat{U}$, the eigenvalues are
  $u_{11},\ldots,u_{nn}$, matching the elimination formula

::: {.notes}
For a real matrix, nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs, so their
product is real. Diagonalizability is not needed. The formula counts roots of
the characteristic polynomial with algebraic multiplicity. Emphasize this as
a forward preview, not as the Deck 07 development.
:::

## Compute only what the problem requires

Use a determinant when the number itself answers the question:

- signed area or volume scaling
- orientation or dimension collapse
- a structural statement about invertibility
- the product of eigenvalues

Use elimination or PLU—not determinant formulas—to solve
$\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$

In floating-point computation, a small determinant depends strongly on scale

By itself, it is not a reliable test for a nearly singular matrix

The [Determinants companion notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH332Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/demonstrations/04-determinants.ipynb)
explores these computations and geometric effects

::: {.key-point}
A determinant [summarizes structure]{.alert}

It does not replace the factorization that computed it
:::

# Matrices of Functions

The entries may vary while the determinant keeps its familiar meaning

- [A determinant can depend on a parameter](#a-determinant-can-depend-on-a-parameter)
- [A Wronskian tests relations among functions](#a-wronskian-tests-relations-among-functions)
- [A Jacobian is the local linear map](#a-jacobian-is-the-local-linear-map)
- [Polar coordinates explain the factor $r$](#polar-coordinates-explain-the-factor-r)
- [Similar formulas answer different questions](#similar-formulas-answer-different-questions)

## A determinant can depend on a parameter

At each fixed $t$, this is an ordinary numerical matrix:

$$
\mat{A}(t)=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&t\\
t&1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\det\bigl(\mat{A}(t)\bigr)=1-t^2
$$

Therefore

\begin{align*}
t\ne\pm1
&\implies \mat{A}(t)\text{ is invertible},\\
t=\pm1
&\implies \mat{A}(t)\text{ collapses a direction}
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
The determinant identifies the [exceptional parameter values]{.alert}
:::

## A Wronskian tests relations among functions

For two differentiable functions,

$$
W(f_1,f_2)(t)
=\det\begin{bmatrix}f_1(t)&f_2(t)\\f_1'(t)&f_2'(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$

For $f_1(t)=\cos t$ and $f_2(t)=\sin t$,

$$
\det\begin{bmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{bmatrix}=1
$$

If $c_1\cos t+c_2\sin t=0$ for every $t$, differentiating gives a
homogeneous system with this invertible coefficient matrix

Hence $c_1=c_2=0$: the functions are linearly independent

::: {.notes}
A nonzero Wronskian at one point proves linear independence. A zero
Wronskian does not generally prove dependence without additional hypotheses.
The coefficients in the linear relation are constants, not functions of $t$.
:::

## A Jacobian is the local linear map

Let $F:\reals^n\to\reals^n$ be differentiable near $\vct{p}$

Its Jacobian has the partial-derivative vectors as columns:

$$
\mat{J}_F(\vct{p})
=\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}&\cdots&\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_n}\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\dfrac{\partial F_n}{\partial x_1}&\cdots&\dfrac{\partial F_n}{\partial x_n}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

For a small displacement $\vct{h}$,

$$
F(\vct{p}+\vct{h})\approx F(\vct{p})+\mat{J}_F(\vct{p})\vct{h}
$$

::: {.key-point}
$\abs{\det\bigl(\mat{J}_F(\vct{p})\bigr)}$ gives local volume scale;
the sign records orientation, and zero signals first-order collapse
:::

## Polar coordinates explain the factor $r$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
$$
F(r,\theta)=
\begin{bmatrix}r\cos\theta\\r\sin\theta\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\mat{J}_F(r,\theta)=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\
\sin\theta&r\cos\theta
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\det\bigl(\mat{J}_F\bigr)=r
$$

For $r>0$, a small coordinate rectangle has image area

$$
\text{area}\approx r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta
$$
:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 520 310" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="A small rectangle in radius-angle coordinates maps to a curved annular-sector patch in the plane.">

the local parallelogram
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
At $r=0$, polar coordinates collapse every angle to the origin and the
Jacobian is singular. The exact image is a curved annular-sector patch; its
first-order approximation is the parallelogram spanned by the two Jacobian
columns.
:::

## Similar formulas answer different questions

| Matrix of derivatives | What its columns represent | What the determinant tells us |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Wronskian | functions and successive derivatives | rules out a constant-coefficient relation |
| Jacobian | responses to coordinate displacements | local scale, orientation, or collapse |

Both use derivatives, but their columns have [different meanings]{.alert}

For a surface $G(u,v)\in\reals^3$, the two Jacobian columns
$G_u$ and $G_v$ are tangent vectors; their spanned area is

$$
\left\lVert G_u\mathbin{\times}G_v\right\rVert
=\sqrt{\det\bigl(\mat{J}_G^{\mathsf T}\mat{J}_G\bigr)}
$$

::: {.notes}
This is only an outlook. Manifolds and tensor calculus are beyond the present
scope. Higher-order derivative information may be organized as tensors, but
the first-order local map here is still represented by a matrix.
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder"}

- $\det(\mat{A})$ is a [signed volume scale factor]{.alert}: magnitude scales
  volume, sign records orientation, and zero means dimension collapse
- Compute determinants by [eliminating to triangular form]{.alert} and tracking swaps and scalings
- PLU stores the needed information in the row permutation and the diagonal of $\mat{U}$
- $\det(\mat{A})\ne0$ exactly when $\mat{A}$ is invertible
- Products multiply determinants<br>Later, eigenvalues will also multiply to the
  determinant
- For matrices of functions, determinants can reveal exceptional parameter
  values, function independence, and local geometric scaling

# What Comes Next

Determinants measure how a matrix transformation changes volume and orientation

- length and distance
- angle and orthogonality
